title: Container exits straight after docker run
summary: The container starts and dies within a second. The exit code tells you which of five very different problems you have.

steps.title: Read the exit code
steps.look: The number in Exited (N). This single number splits the problem five ways, and every branch below has a different fix. Do not skip to the logs before you have it.

signals.means: Docker itself refused to start the container. The error is in your run flags, not the image.
The entrypoint was found but could not be executed. Missing execute bit, or a CRLF line ending in a shell script.
The entrypoint was not found at all. Wrong path, or no shell in a distroless or scratch base.
SIGKILL. Either the memory limit was hit or something sent a kill.
It ran and finished normally. There was no long-running process to keep it alive.
The application itself chose to exit. The reason is in the logs.

steps.title: Read the logs it managed to write
steps.look: The first error, not the last. If this is empty, the process died before it could log anything, which points back at the entrypoint rather than the app.

signals.means: The process cannot read a path or bind a port as its user.
A path in the entrypoint or a required file is absent from the image.
Empty. The container died before logging, so the fault is in the entrypoint or the run flags.

steps.title: Check what the image says it should run
steps.look: Compare this against what actually exists in the image. A null Cmd with a shell-form Entrypoint is a common source of exit 127.

steps.title: Open a shell in the image to see what is really there
steps.note: Creates a new container. It is removed on exit because of --rm, but it does consume a container slot and will pull the image if absent. If this fails with 'exec sh not found', the base image has no shell at all, which is itself the answer.
steps.look: Whether the entrypoint file exists, whether it is executable, and whether the interpreter on its first line is present.

causes.cause: Exit 0. The image's command finished. A container lives exactly as long as PID 1.
causes.fix: Run the real server process in the foreground, not backgrounded or daemonised. A CMD that ends is a container that ends.

causes.cause: Exit 127. The entrypoint path does not exist inside the image.
causes.fix: Check the path in the Dockerfile against the built layers. On distroless or scratch there is no /bin/sh, so shell-form CMD will always fail.

causes.cause: Exit 126. The file exists but cannot be run. Usually a missing execute bit, or a script saved with Windows CRLF line endings.
causes.fix: Add RUN chmod +x in the Dockerfile. If you edited the script on Windows, convert it to LF — CRLF makes the shebang unresolvable.

causes.cause: Exit 137. SIGKILL, almost always the memory limit.
causes.fix: Raise --memory, or fix the allocation. Check OOMKilled in inspect to confirm it was memory rather than an external kill.

causes.cause: Exit 125. The Docker daemon rejected the run request before the image was involved.
causes.fix: Re-read the docker run line. A bad mount path, an unknown flag, or a port already bound will all produce this.

verify: docker ps shows the container in Up state, not Restarting.
The status stays Up across at least a minute.
docker logs shows the application's normal startup output.
escalate: First 50 lines of docker logs, or a note that it was empty
Entrypoint, Cmd and User from image inspect, plus the full docker run line

title: docker pull fails with denied or unauthorized
summary: The registry refused you. Whether that is authentication, authorisation, or a typo in the tag depends on the exact wording.

steps.title: Read the exact refusal
steps.look: The precise wording. 'denied' and 'unauthorized' and 'manifest unknown' are three different problems that look identical at a glance.

signals.means: You are authenticated fine. That tag does not exist in that repository.
You are not logged in to this registry at all.

signals.match: (?i)denied: requested access to the resource is denied
signals.means: You are logged in, but this account cannot read this repository.
TLS trust failure, not an auth failure. The registry's CA is not trusted by your Docker daemon.
You never reached the registry. This is DNS or egress, not credentials.

steps.title: Check which registries you are actually logged in to
steps.look: Whether {registry} appears in the auths block. A credential helper means the token lives in Windows Credential Manager rather than the file, so an empty auths block is not proof you are logged out.

steps.title: Confirm the tag exists before blaming credentials
steps.look: A manifest means the tag is real and readable. An error here with a valid login means the tag is wrong or was garbage-collected.

causes.cause: No credentials cached for this registry.
causes.fix: docker login {registry}. If a credential helper is configured, log in through that rather than storing a token in plain config.json.

causes.cause: Authenticated, but the account lacks pull rights on that repository.
causes.fix: Ask the registry owner for read access on that path. A token scoped to another project produces exactly this message.

causes.cause: The tag does not exist. Very often a typo, or a tag that was cleaned up by a retention policy.
causes.fix: List the available tags and pick a real one. Prefer pinning by digest for anything that matters.

causes.cause: The registry's certificate is not trusted by the Docker daemon.
causes.fix: Install the CA into the daemon's trust store. Do not add the host to insecure-registries to make this go away.

causes.cause: The registry host did not resolve or did not answer.
causes.fix: Check DNS and any corporate proxy. Docker reads proxy settings from its own config, not from your shell environment.

verify: docker pull completes and reports a digest.
docker images lists the image locally.
A fresh shell can repeat the pull without logging in again.
escalate: The verbatim error line from docker pull
Which registry and repository path, with the tag
Whether docker manifest inspect succeeds or fails

title: no space left on device
summary: Builds or containers fail on disk. Find out what is consuming it before you reclaim anything, because the fast fix deletes real data.

steps.title: Find out what is actually using the space
steps.look: The RECLAIMABLE column per category. Build cache is usually the largest and the safest to drop. Volumes are usually the smallest and the most dangerous.

signals.means: Read the build cache line specifically. On a CI-style machine it is often most of the total and costs nothing but rebuild time.
Volumes hold real data. Nothing in this runbook should delete them without you knowing what is inside.

steps.title: Check whether the host disk is full rather than Docker
steps.note: Starts a throwaway container and mounts the host root read-write into it. It only runs df, but anything with this mount could write to the host filesystem. On Docker Desktop for Windows this inspects the Linux VM's disk, not your C: drive.
steps.look: Whether the filesystem holding /var/lib/docker is full, or whether something else on the host filled the disk and Docker is just the victim.

steps.title: Reclaim the build cache only
steps.note: Permanently deletes build cache older than seven days. Nothing running is affected and no image or volume is touched, but your next build of an affected image will be slow because it has to rebuild those layers. This cannot be undone.
steps.look: The reclaimed total at the end. Re-run docker system df to confirm the space actually came back.

steps.title: Remove stopped containers and dangling images
steps.cmd: docker container prune && docker image prune
steps.note: Deletes every stopped container and every untagged image. A stopped container that someone intended to restart or inspect is gone, along with its writable layer and anything written outside a volume. Run docker ps -a first and read the list. Never use docker system prune -a --volumes here — that also removes named volumes and is how people lose databases.
steps.look: The list of deleted IDs. If you see something you recognise, stop and check what it was before continuing.

causes.cause: BuildKit cache has accumulated across many builds.
causes.fix: Prune with a time filter rather than wholesale, and set a cache ceiling in the daemon config so it bounds itself.

causes.cause: Exited containers are retained along with their writable layers.
causes.fix: Prune them, and add --rm to throwaway docker run commands so they clean up on exit.

causes.cause: Rebuilt tags leave the previous image untagged but still on disk.
causes.fix: docker image prune. Schedule it rather than doing it in a panic mid-incident.

causes.cause: Anonymous volumes from removed containers persist and are never cleaned automatically.
causes.fix: Inspect each one before deleting anything. Use named volumes so ownership is obvious from the name.

causes.cause: Container JSON log files grew unbounded because no rotation was configured.
causes.fix: Set max-size and max-file in the daemon's log-opts. This is the fix that stops it recurring.

verify: docker system df shows meaningful free space.
The build or container that was failing now succeeds.
Log rotation is configured, so the same disk does not fill again next week.
escalate: Whether anything was pruned, and exactly which command was run

title: Container cannot reach another container or the internet
summary: Connection refused or name not resolving from inside a container. Work outward: name, then network membership, then egress.

inputs.label: What it is trying to reach

steps.title: Check whether the name resolves from inside the container
steps.look: An IP means DNS is fine and the problem is the port or the listener. No output means Docker's embedded DNS does not know that name.

signals.means: The name did not resolve. Either the containers are not on the same user-defined network, or the name is wrong.
DNS is working. Move to the port and the listener.

steps.title: Compare which networks each container is attached to
steps.look: The same user-defined network name in both. The default bridge gives no DNS between containers at all, which is the single most common cause of this symptom.

signals.means: On the default bridge, container name resolution does not work. You need a user-defined network.

steps.title: Check that the target is listening where you think
steps.look: Whether it is bound to 0.0.0.0 or to 127.0.0.1. A process bound to localhost inside a container is unreachable from every other container, no matter how correct the network is.

signals.means: It is only listening on loopback inside its own namespace. Nothing outside that container can reach it.

steps.title: Test egress to the outside world
steps.cmd: docker exec {container} sh -c "getent hosts registry-1.docker.io || echo DNS_FAIL"
steps.look: DNS_FAIL means the container has no working resolver, which usually points at a host DNS or corporate proxy setting that Docker did not inherit.

causes.cause: The containers are not attached to a common user-defined network.
causes.fix: Put both on the same named network. In Compose this is automatic within a project, so this usually means they are in two different projects.

causes.cause: Both are on the default bridge network, which has no embedded DNS for container names.
causes.fix: Create a user-defined network and attach both. Only user-defined networks give name-based service discovery.

causes.cause: The target process listens on 127.0.0.1 inside its own network namespace.
causes.fix: Bind it to 0.0.0.0 in the application's own configuration. No Docker flag can work around this.

causes.cause: The client is dialling the published host port rather than the container port.
causes.fix: Between containers, use the container's internal port. Published ports are for traffic arriving from the host.

causes.cause: Corporate DNS or proxy settings were not inherited by the daemon.
causes.fix: Set dns in the daemon config, or pass --dns. Docker does not read your shell's proxy variables.

verify: getent hosts resolves the target name from inside the container.
A connection to the target's internal port succeeds.
The same works after both containers are restarted.
escalate: Networks block from inspect for both containers

title: port is already allocated
summary: docker run fails because something already holds the host port.

steps.title: Find which container holds it
steps.look: A container name means Docker itself is holding it, and you can stop that container. Nothing means a host process has it.

signals.means: A container already publishes this port.
No container has it, so a host process does.

steps.title: Find the host process holding it
steps.look: The PID in the last column. Look it up in Task Manager before killing anything.

steps.title: Check for a stopped container still reserving it
steps.look: On some versions a container in a bad state keeps the mapping. Removing it releases the port.

causes.cause: Another container publishes the same host port.
causes.fix: Stop it, or publish this one on a different host port. The container port does not need to change.

causes.cause: A non-Docker process on the host owns the port.
causes.fix: Stop that process, or pick another host port.

causes.cause: A dead container is still holding the reservation.
causes.fix: docker rm the container. If it persists, restart the Docker daemon.

verify: docker run starts and publishes the port.
The service answers on the host port.

title: Permission denied on a mounted volume
summary: The container cannot read or write a bind-mounted path. It is almost always a UID mismatch.

steps.title: Find which user the container runs as
steps.look: An empty user means root, which rarely hits permission errors. A numeric UID that does not own the host directory is the usual cause.

signals.means: The root filesystem is read-only by design. Writes outside a volume will always fail.

steps.title: Check the ownership the container sees
steps.look: The numeric owner UID, not the name. Names differ between host and container; only the number matters.

steps.title: Check the mount type
steps.look: A bind mount inherits host permissions exactly. A named volume is initialised from the image and usually avoids this entirely.

signals.means: Bind mount, so host ownership applies directly.
Mounted read-only. The flag, not the permissions.

causes.cause: The container's UID does not own the host directory.
causes.fix: Either chown the host directory to that UID, or run the container as the UID that owns it with --user.

causes.cause: The mount was declared read-only.
causes.fix: Drop the :ro suffix if writes are genuinely needed.

causes.cause: The container's root filesystem is read-only.
causes.fix: Mount a writable volume at the path that needs writes. Keep the rootfs read-only; it is a good default.

causes.cause: SELinux is blocking the bind mount on the host.
causes.fix: Add the :z or :Z suffix to the mount. Not applicable on Docker Desktop for Windows.

verify: The container reads and writes the path successfully.
The fix is in the compose file or run command, not a manual chmod that will be lost.
escalate: ls -ldn output from inside the container

title: Docker build reruns every step instead of using cache
summary: Builds that should take seconds take minutes. One early layer is invalidating everything after it.

steps.title: Build with plain progress and find the first miss
steps.look: The first step that is not CACHED. Everything after it is invalidated by definition, so only that first miss matters.

signals.means: Copying the whole context early invalidates the cache on any file change.

steps.title: Check how large the context being sent is
steps.look: A large context means .dockerignore is missing entries. node_modules and .git are the usual culprits.

steps.title: Check whether .dockerignore exists at all
steps.look: Its absence is the single most common reason builds are slow. Without it, every local file change busts the cache.

causes.cause: COPY . happens before dependency installation.
causes.fix: Copy only the manifest files, install dependencies, then copy the rest. Dependencies then cache independently of source changes.

causes.cause: No .dockerignore, so the whole directory is context.
causes.fix: Add one covering .git, node_modules, build output and local env files.

causes.cause: An early RUN embeds a date or fetches something that changes each run.
causes.fix: Move it later, or pin what it fetches.

causes.cause: CI starts with an empty cache every run.
causes.fix: Use a registry cache with --cache-from and --cache-to.

verify: A rebuild with no source changes is almost entirely CACHED.
Context transfer is small.
escalate: The plain-progress output showing the first cache miss

title: Compose service never becomes healthy
summary: docker compose up hangs on a dependency, or a service restarts forever waiting on another.

steps.title: See which service is failing its health check
steps.look: The STATUS column. 'starting' for a long time means the health check has not passed yet; 'unhealthy' means it has failed its retries.

signals.means: The health check ran and failed repeatedly.
Still inside start_period. It may just need a longer allowance.

steps.title: Read the health check's actual output
steps.look: The Log array holds the last few probe results with their exit codes and output. This is the actual reason, not a guess.

steps.title: Read the service's own logs
steps.look: Whether the process is genuinely failing or simply slower to start than the health check allows.

causes.cause: The health check command is wrong for the image.
causes.fix: Test it manually with docker exec first. curl is often absent from slim images.

causes.cause: The service needs longer to start than start_period allows.
causes.fix: Raise start_period. It exists precisely so slow starts are not counted as failures.

causes.cause: depends_on without condition only waits for start, not for health.
causes.fix: Use condition: service_healthy so the dependent service actually waits.

causes.cause: The application is genuinely failing to start.
causes.fix: Fix the app. The health check is reporting correctly.

verify: docker compose ps shows every service healthy.
A fresh docker compose up reaches healthy without manual intervention.

title: exec format error when the container starts
summary: The image was built for a different CPU architecture than the machine running it.

steps.title: Compare the image architecture against the host
steps.look: The two strings must match. arm64 against amd64 is the classic case, usually an image built on an Apple Silicon laptop and run on a cloud VM.

signals.means: Architecture mismatch. The binary cannot execute on this CPU.
OS mismatch. A Linux image cannot run in Windows container mode.

steps.title: Check which platforms the registry actually offers
steps.look: A manifest list with several platform entries means a matching one exists and Docker picked wrong. A single entry means only one was ever published.

steps.title: Check whether a shebang is the real problem
steps.look: exec format error also occurs when a script has no shebang line, or has a Windows CRLF line ending that corrupts it. This is a different cause with the same message.

steps.title: Pull explicitly for this platform
steps.look: The pull succeeds and inspect now reports the expected architecture.
steps.note: Downloads another copy of the image and replaces the local tag reference. Disk usage grows and any container built from the previous local tag still uses the old one until recreated. If no matching platform was published this simply fails.

causes.cause: The image was built for a different CPU architecture.
causes.fix: Build multi-platform with buildx, or build on the target architecture. Apple Silicon defaults to arm64 and this catches teams constantly.

causes.cause: A Linux image on a Windows container host.
causes.fix: Switch Docker Desktop to Linux containers.

causes.cause: The entrypoint script has no shebang or has CRLF endings.
causes.fix: Add #!/bin/sh and save with LF endings. Set .gitattributes so Git does not convert it.

causes.cause: Only one platform was published.
causes.fix: Rebuild and push a manifest list covering both.

verify: The container starts and stays running.
Image architecture matches the host.
CI publishes every platform the fleet actually runs.
escalate: The entrypoint's first line if a script

title: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
summary: Every docker command fails before reaching a container. The client cannot talk to the engine.
aliases: cannot connect to the docker daemon

steps.title: Check whether the client can reach the engine at all
steps.look: The Client block always prints. If the Server block is missing, the client is fine and the engine is not reachable.

signals.match: (?i)(failed|error|unable) (during |to )?connect.*docker|cannot connect to the docker daemon|docker_engine|docker\.sock.*(no such file|refused)|Is the docker daemon running
signals.means: The client is fine but the engine is not reachable. On Windows that almost always means Docker Desktop is not running.
The engine is running but your user cannot use its socket.

signals.match: (?i)the system cannot find the file specified|no such host|npipe.*not found
signals.means: The named pipe does not exist, so the engine has not created it. The engine is stopped.
A Server block is present, so the engine is reachable. Whatever failed is not the daemon.

steps.title: Check whether Docker Desktop is actually running
steps.look: On Windows the engine lives inside Docker Desktop. No process means nothing to connect to, regardless of the client.

signals.means: The process is running. If the client still cannot connect, the engine inside it may still be starting or may have crashed.
Docker Desktop is not running at all. Start it and wait for the engine to report ready.

steps.title: Check what endpoint the client is trying
steps.look: The active context's endpoint. A leftover context pointing at a remote host or an old WSL distro produces exactly this error while Desktop runs happily.

signals.means: Pointing at a remote engine that may be unreachable.

steps.title: Switch back to the default context
steps.look: docker version now prints a Server block.
steps.note: Changes which engine every subsequent docker command talks to, for this user. Containers on the previously selected engine keep running but become invisible from this shell until you switch back.

causes.cause: Docker Desktop is not running.
causes.fix: Start it and wait for the engine to report ready. It takes longer than the tray icon suggests.

causes.cause: The active context points at an unreachable engine.
causes.fix: Switch to default. Contexts persist and are easy to forget.

causes.cause: Your user is not permitted to use the socket.
causes.fix: On Linux add the user to the docker group and start a new session.

causes.cause: The WSL backend distro is not running.
causes.fix: Restart WSL, then Docker Desktop.

causes.cause: The engine started and died.
causes.fix: Read the Docker Desktop diagnostic logs. Disk exhaustion on the VM is a common cause.

verify: docker version prints a Server block.
docker ps returns without error.
The active context is the one you intend.

title: Container is running but marked unhealthy
summary: The process is alive but the health check keeps failing, so dependent services never start.

steps.title: Read the health check's recorded output
steps.look: The Log array holds the last few probe attempts with exit codes and output. This is the actual reason rather than an inference.

signals.means: The health check command does not exist inside the image.
The app is not listening on the probed port yet or at all.
The command ran and reported failure.

steps.title: Read the configured check
steps.look: The test, interval, timeout, retries and start period. A start period shorter than the real startup time guarantees early failures.

steps.title: Run the check yourself inside the container
steps.look: The real exit code and output. Running it by hand removes all ambiguity about what the daemon is seeing.

steps.title: Check whether the tool the check uses even exists
steps.cmd: docker exec {container} sh -c "which curl wget nc 2>/dev/null; echo done"
steps.look: Slim and distroless images frequently lack curl. A health check calling a missing binary fails forever and looks like an application problem.

causes.cause: The health check calls a binary the image does not contain.
causes.fix: Install it, or use something the image has. Many runtimes can check their own health without an external tool.

causes.cause: The app is not listening on the probed port.
causes.fix: Confirm the port and that it binds 0.0.0.0 rather than localhost.

causes.cause: The container needs longer to start than start_period allows.
causes.fix: Raise start_period. Failures during it are not counted, which is exactly what it is for.

causes.cause: The application really is unhealthy.
causes.fix: Read its logs. The check is doing its job.

causes.cause: The check probes a different port than the app uses.
causes.fix: Use the container's internal port, not the published host port.

verify: docker ps shows healthy.
It stays healthy through a normal workload.
Dependent services start as expected.
escalate: Result of running the test manually

title: Variables in the compose file are empty
summary: A ${VAR} in docker-compose.yml resolves to nothing and the container starts misconfigured.
aliases: warn the variable is not set

steps.title: Render the fully resolved configuration
steps.look: Compose prints what it will actually use after all substitution. Anything empty here will be empty in the container, and warnings appear at the top.

signals.means: Compose could not resolve a variable and substituted an empty string.
A literal placeholder survived, meaning it was escaped or malformed.

steps.title: Check the .env file location
steps.look: Compose reads .env from the directory it is invoked in, not from where the compose file lives. Running from a parent directory silently loses it.

steps.title: Understand which mechanism you are using
steps.look: env_file passes variables into the container. The .env file substitutes into the compose file itself. They are completely different and are constantly confused.

signals.means: env_file populates the container's environment. It does not substitute into the YAML.

steps.title: Check what the container actually received
steps.look: The final answer. Empty here with a correct compose config means the variable was never mapped into the service.

causes.cause: No .env file in the working directory.
causes.fix: Create it there, or pass --env-file explicitly. Compose does not search upward.

causes.cause: Using env_file where .env substitution was intended.
causes.fix: For values inside the YAML use .env. For values inside the container use environment or env_file.

causes.cause: The variable is available to compose but not passed to the service.
causes.fix: Add it under environment on the service. Compose does not forward your shell environment automatically.

causes.cause: The placeholder was escaped with $$.
causes.fix: $$ produces a literal dollar sign. Use a single $ for substitution.

causes.cause: Quotes in the .env file are being taken literally.
causes.fix: Do not quote values in .env unless the quotes are part of the value.

verify: docker compose config shows real values with no warnings.
printenv inside the container returns the value.
It works from a clean checkout.
escalate: Whether .env exists in the invocation directory
Result of printenv inside the container

title: Docker network conflicts with the corporate network
summary: Creating a network fails, or containers break VPN or internal-host access after starting.

steps.title: Read the conflict error
steps.look: Docker names the overlapping pool. It allocates from 172.17.0.0/16 upward by default, which collides with many corporate ranges.

signals.match: (?i)Pool overlaps with other one|address already in use
signals.means: The requested range collides with an existing network.

steps.title: List the subnets already allocated
steps.cmd: docker network ls --format "{{.Name}}" | ForEach-Object { docker network inspect $_ --format '{{.Name}}' ; docker network inspect $_ | findstr Subnet }
steps.look: Every Docker network's range. Stale networks from deleted compose projects often hold ranges nothing uses.

steps.title: Compare against the host's own routes
steps.look: Whether a corporate or VPN route covers the same range. If so, containers will capture traffic meant for internal hosts and the symptom looks like a VPN failure.

steps.title: Remove unused networks to free ranges
steps.look: The reclaimed list. Recreate your network afterwards and confirm the range.
steps.note: Deletes every network not currently used by a container. Any stopped container that expected a custom network will fail to start until it is recreated, and fixed IP assignments on those networks are lost. Run docker network ls first and recognise what is listed.

causes.cause: The default address pools are used up or collide.
causes.fix: Set default-address-pools in the daemon configuration to a range your corporate network does not use.

causes.cause: A Docker network overlaps a VPN route.
causes.fix: Pin the network to an explicit subnet outside the corporate range. Do this in the compose file so it is reproducible.

causes.cause: Old networks hold ranges nothing needs.
causes.fix: Prune them. Compose leaves networks behind when projects are renamed.

causes.cause: Two compose projects declare the same explicit subnet.
causes.fix: Give each project its own range.

verify: The network is created with a non-conflicting range.
Containers reach both the internet and internal hosts.
The VPN still works with containers running.
escalate: The host's routing table for the conflicting range

title: COPY fails with file not found during build
summary: The file exists on disk but the build cannot see it. Context, ignore rules or stage boundaries.
aliases: no such file or directory copy

steps.title: Read which path the build could not find
steps.look: The path in the error is relative to the build context root, never to the Dockerfile's own location. That distinction causes most of these.

signals.means: The path does not exist relative to the context root.
Copying from a build stage that does not produce that path.

steps.title: Check the context root being sent
steps.look: The final argument to docker build sets the context. Building with a context of . while the file sits above it means the file is simply not available.

steps.title: Check whether .dockerignore excludes it
steps.look: An ignored file is invisible to COPY even though it exists. A broad pattern such as dist/ or *.jar is the usual cause and produces a confusing error.

steps.title: Check the path exists relative to the context
steps.look: Run this from the same directory you pass as the build context. If it fails here, the Dockerfile was never going to find it.

causes.cause: The path is relative to the Dockerfile rather than the context.
causes.fix: Paths in COPY are always relative to the context root. Adjust the path or the context.

causes.cause: .dockerignore excludes the file.
causes.fix: Add a negation pattern, or narrow the exclusion.

causes.cause: The artifact has not been produced.
causes.fix: Build it before docker build, or move the build into an earlier stage.

causes.cause: COPY --from references a path the stage does not create.
causes.fix: Check the earlier stage's working directory and output path.

causes.cause: The file is above the context directory.
causes.fix: COPY cannot reach outside the context, ever. Move the file in or widen the context.

verify: The build completes.
The file is present in the image at the expected path.
It builds the same way in CI from a clean checkout.

title: docker logs shows nothing
summary: The container is running but produces no log output, so you are debugging blind.

steps.title: Confirm the container is producing anything at all
steps.look: Timestamps reveal whether output is old or absent. Output that stops at startup usually means buffering rather than silence.

signals.means: Nothing captured at all.

steps.title: Check which logging driver is in use
steps.look: docker logs only works with json-file or journald. With any other driver it returns nothing by design, and that is not a fault.

signals.means: Logging is disabled for this container.
Logs go elsewhere. docker logs cannot read them.

steps.title: Check whether the app writes to a file instead of stdout
steps.look: Applications configured for a traditional server write to files. Only stdout and stderr reach docker logs.

steps.title: Check for output buffering
steps.look: Python buffers stdout when it is not a terminal, so output can sit unseen for a long time. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 fixes it and is why so many images set it.

causes.cause: The logging driver is none.
causes.fix: Change it to json-file. Someone probably set this to save disk.

causes.cause: Logs are shipped to a remote system.
causes.fix: Read them there. docker logs is not broken.

causes.cause: The application logs to a file.
causes.fix: Reconfigure it to stdout, or symlink the file to /dev/stdout.

causes.cause: Output is buffered because stdout is not a terminal.
causes.fix: Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, or the equivalent for the runtime.

causes.cause: Log rotation removed the output.
causes.fix: Raise max-size and max-file in the log options.

verify: docker logs shows current application output.
New output appears without delay.
The driver suits how you actually read logs.
escalate: Whether the app writes to files

title: Image is far larger than expected
summary: Slow pulls, slow deploys and wasted registry storage. Usually one layer.

steps.title: See the size of every layer
steps.look: The largest layer and the instruction that made it. One layer usually accounts for most of the size.

signals.means: A package install layer. Cleaning in a later layer does not shrink it.
The whole context was copied in.

steps.title: Compare against the base image
steps.cmd: docker image inspect {image} --format '{{.Size}}' && docker image ls
steps.look: How much is base and how much is yours. A large base means switching to slim or alpine gains more than any other change.

steps.title: Check whether build tooling is in the final image
steps.cmd: docker run --rm {image} sh -c "which gcc make git npm 2>/dev/null; echo ---"
steps.look: Compilers and package managers in a runtime image mean multi-stage is missing. They are also an attack surface.

steps.title: Check for a .dockerignore
steps.look: Without one, .git and node_modules are copied in. This routinely adds hundreds of megabytes nobody intended.

causes.cause: Package manager caches are baked into a layer.
causes.fix: Clean in the same RUN instruction. A later cleanup layer cannot remove data from an earlier one.

causes.cause: COPY . brought in everything.
causes.fix: Add .dockerignore and copy only what the image needs.

causes.cause: Build tooling ships in the runtime image.
causes.fix: Use multi-stage and copy only the artifact into a slim final stage.

causes.cause: The base image is large.
causes.fix: Move to a slim or distroless base. Test carefully; distroless has no shell.

causes.cause: Credentials were copied in during build.
causes.fix: They are recoverable from the layers. Rotate them and use build secrets instead.

verify: The image is meaningfully smaller.
No build tooling in the runtime image.
Pull time improved in a real deployment.
escalate: Output of docker history sorted by size

title: Container restarts endlessly
summary: A restart policy keeps bringing back a container that immediately dies.

steps.title: Confirm the restart count is climbing
steps.look: A rising count with policy always means Docker is masking a failure that would otherwise be obvious.

signals.means: Docker will restart it forever regardless of why it dies.
Restarting only on non-zero exit, which is more informative.

steps.title: Read the logs from before the last restart
steps.look: Docker keeps logs across restarts in the same container, so the failure from previous attempts is still here.

steps.title: Read the last exit code
steps.look: The same exit-code logic as a container that will not start. OOMKilled true means memory, not the application.

steps.title: Stop the loop so you can inspect it calmly
steps.look: The container stays stopped. You can now inspect it without it disappearing under you.
steps.note: Changes the restart policy on the running container and then stops it. The service stays down until you start it again, so do not do this on something serving traffic without arranging cover. The policy change persists until you set it back.

causes.cause: The restart policy hides a real failure.
causes.fix: Read the logs. Restarting is not a fix and the exit code tells you the category.

causes.cause: It starts before something it needs.
causes.fix: Add a retry with backoff in the application. depends_on does not wait for readiness by default.

causes.cause: The memory limit is too low.
causes.fix: Raise it or fix the leak. The container will loop forever otherwise.

causes.cause: Configuration is wrong, so it fails at startup every time.
causes.fix: Fix the config. Every restart fails identically.

causes.cause: It cannot bind its port.
causes.fix: Follow the port-already-allocated runbook.

verify: The restart count stops climbing.
The container stays Up for a sustained period.
The underlying failure was fixed, not restarted past.
escalate: The last exit code and OOM flag

title: Builds are extremely slow
summary: Beyond cache misses, a few specific things make builds crawl.

steps.title: Find where the time goes
steps.look: Each step's duration. One dominating step tells you where to look, and it is often not the one you assumed.

signals.means: Sending the context is slow, meaning it is too big.
Dependency installation dominates. It should be cached.

steps.title: Measure the context size
steps.look: Anything above a few megabytes suggests .dockerignore is missing entries. The context is sent before the build starts.

steps.title: Check whether BuildKit is enabled
steps.look: BuildKit parallelises independent stages and skips unused ones. The legacy builder does neither.

steps.title: Check for platform emulation
steps.look: Building linux/amd64 on an arm64 machine through QEMU is roughly ten times slower. This is a common hidden cause.

causes.cause: The build context is large.
causes.fix: Add .dockerignore covering .git, node_modules and build output.

causes.cause: Dependencies reinstall every build.
causes.fix: Copy the lockfile, install, then copy source. Ordering is everything.

causes.cause: Using the legacy builder.
causes.fix: Enable BuildKit. It is the default in current Docker but can be disabled.

causes.cause: Cross-platform build through QEMU.
causes.fix: Build natively on the target architecture, or use a remote builder.

causes.cause: CI starts cold every time.
causes.fix: Use --cache-from and --cache-to against a registry.

causes.cause: One huge stage does everything.
causes.fix: Split into stages so independent work runs in parallel.

verify: Build time is meaningfully lower.
A no-change rebuild is almost entirely cached.
Context transfer is fast.
escalate: Whether BuildKit and native architecture are in use

title: Cannot remove a container or image
summary: Removal is refused because something still references it.

steps.title: Read what is blocking removal
steps.look: The conflict message names the blocker. Running container, dependent child image and in-use image are three different situations.

signals.means: It is still running. Stop it first.
A container references the image.
Another image was built on top of this one.

steps.title: Find which containers reference the image
steps.look: Every container built from it, including stopped ones. Stopped containers hold images just as firmly as running ones.

steps.title: Find images built on top of it
steps.look: Child images. The parent cannot be removed while any child exists.

steps.title: Stop and remove the container properly
steps.look: The container is gone from docker ps -a. Volumes it used remain unless you also remove them.
steps.note: Sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after the timeout, then deletes the container and its writable layer. Anything written inside the container but not to a volume is permanently lost. Check what is mounted before running this.

causes.cause: The container is running.
causes.fix: Stop it first, or use -f if you are certain. -f sends SIGKILL with no clean shutdown.

causes.cause: A container references the image.
causes.fix: Remove the containers first. Stopped ones count.

causes.cause: Another image was built from it.
causes.fix: Remove the children first, or use -f to untag only.

causes.cause: A volume is still referenced.
causes.fix: Remove the containers using it. Volumes outlive containers deliberately.

causes.cause: You want to clean untagged images.
causes.fix: docker image prune targets exactly those.

verify: The container or image is removed.
Nothing that was still needed was deleted.
Disk usage reflects the removal.

title: DNS does not work inside containers
summary: The container has network access but cannot resolve names.

steps.title: Test resolution from inside
steps.cmd: docker exec {container} sh -c "getent hosts github.com || echo FAIL"
steps.look: Whether external resolution works at all. FAIL with working connectivity to an IP address isolates it to DNS.

signals.means: No external resolution.

steps.title: Read the container's resolver configuration
steps.look: On a user-defined network you should see 127.0.0.11, Docker's embedded resolver. Anything else means it is using host or explicit DNS.

signals.means: Docker's embedded DNS, which forwards to the host's resolvers.
Public DNS, which corporate networks often block.

steps.title: Check the host can resolve
steps.look: Docker's embedded resolver forwards to the host's configured servers. If the host cannot resolve, no container will.

steps.title: Check for a VPN changing the host's resolvers
steps.look: Connecting a VPN after Docker started leaves containers pointing at the pre-VPN resolvers, which is a very common cause.

causes.cause: The host's resolvers are unreachable from the container.
causes.fix: Restart the container so it picks up current settings, or set dns explicitly.

causes.cause: Public DNS is blocked by the corporate network.
causes.fix: Configure the daemon with the internal resolvers.

causes.cause: The VPN changed the host's DNS after the container started.
causes.fix: Restart the container. resolv.conf is written at creation.

causes.cause: On the default bridge, container names do not resolve.
causes.fix: Use a user-defined network for name-based discovery.

causes.cause: A search domain is appended unexpectedly.
causes.fix: Check the search line. It can turn an external lookup into an internal one.

verify: Names resolve from inside the container.
Both internal and external names work.
It survives a container restart.
escalate: Contents of resolv.conf inside the container
